design_detail: Short communication. Secondary analysis of the US National Surveys on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), 2002-2016, through online cross-tabulations of the public Restricted-use Data Analysis System (RDAS) for seven year-pairs: 2002-03, 2004-05, 2006-07, 2008-09, 2010-11, 2012-13 and 2015-16 (2014 is not among them). Respondents who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before the interview were divided into powder-only initiates (never used crack) and powder-then-crack initiates (crack begun after powder; NSDUH staff confirmed there were no crack-only or crack-then-powder initiates). For each year-pair the survey-weighted proportion who had become DSM-IV cocaine dependence cases between onset and interview (called an attack rate, an incidence proportion over 1-12 months), and the proportion reporting each of 21 dependence-related side effect problems and experiences (SEPE), were estimated with Taylor-series 95% confidence intervals; the seven year-pair estimates were then summarized by meta-analysis (fixed effects unless a heterogeneity chi-square was significant at 0.05, then random effects). No covariates, by design.
can_establish: How often people in US households who had started cocaine within the previous 12 months, in 2002-2016, met DSM-IV cocaine dependence criteria and reported each of 21 dependence-related problems by the time of interview, separately for those who had used only powder and those who had gone on to crack, as survey-weighted proportions with intervals.
cannot_establish: That smoking crack causes the higher proportions (the authors give pre-existing susceptibility and dependence that precedes crack as equally cogent explanations, and the items do not ask which form caused a problem); a risk per month of use (time since onset, which ranges up to 12 months, is not reported for either subgroup); risks for people outside households and group quarters or for people who start with crack; or which of the 21 problems each bar in Fig. 2 shows, because the item wording is only in the online supplement (not read).

sample.recruitment: Household survey: NSDUH multistage area probability samples of US civilian non-institutionalized residents aged 12 and over, covering households and non-institutional group quarters (homeless shelters, college dormitories), each year more than 50,000 people with participation above 65% (PDF p. 3, 2.1, 1st paragraph). The authors analysed the public RDAS year-pair files online; the Michigan State University IRB judged this not human subjects research (PDF p. 3, 2.1, 2nd paragraph). The abstract's 3488 and 275 are unweighted totals; per year-pair the Methods give unweighted effective sample sizes back-calculated from the RDAS output, 194-590 powder-only and 9-96 powder-then-crack initiates (PDF p. 1; PDF p. 3, 2.3, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cocaine initiates (any form) with onset less than 12 months before assessment. Powder-only: excludes anyone who had tried crack even once. Powder-then-crack: crack begun after powder, including first crack use in the same 12 months as first powder use (PDF p. 3, 2.2, 1st paragraph; PDF p. 2, Fig. 1 footnotes).
sample.demographics: Not reported: no age, sex, ethnicity or other drug use is given for either subgroup. Fig. 1 gives weighted projections of new initiates per year: powder-only between 597,000 (2012-13) and 1,017,000 (2015-16); powder-then-crack falling from 113,000 (2002-03) to 16,000 (2015-16) (PDF p. 2).
sample.selection_effects: Frame of non-institutionalized civilians in dwellings and group quarters; people in institutions are outside it. The authors note that initiates may be missed through flaws in sampling frames or differential non-participation, and that some assessments may be incomplete when dependence has begun (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 7th paragraph). The subgroups are defined by what happened after onset: to be counted as a powder-then-crack initiate a person had to start crack within the same 12 months, which takes time and continued use, so the two groups may differ in time since onset and in amount of use, neither of which is reported.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in audio computer-assisted self-interviews (ACASI): forms of cocaine ever used and time of first use relative to the interview, using standardized RDAS initiation variables (PDF p. 3, 2.1 and 2.2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported. Frequency of use was deliberately not used as a covariate, because the authors regard it as lying on the path from crack use to dependence and as being driven up by dependence (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 8th paragraph). Powder use is described as mainly nasal insufflation in the Introduction (PDF p. 1); route was not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured or analysed; the authors mention prior use of other drugs, including opioids, as a possible antecedent of crack onset and note that recall and reporting errors are likely among initiates who use several drugs (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 5th and 7th paragraphs).

comparison.controls: Powder-only initiates against powder-then-crack initiates, unadjusted. The comparison with heroin (about 30% dependent within 12 months) is with a separate published estimate (Rivera et al., 2018), not with data analysed here.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: All characteristics before first cocaine use (other drug use, psychiatric history, social circumstances, age at onset); the authors name pre-existing susceptibility as one of three explanations for the crack-associated excess (PDF p. 3, Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: NSDUH ACASI cocaine module: 21 items on side effect problems and experiences with cocaine used in any form, without asking whether powder or crack caused them; DSM-IV cocaine dependence cases identified from these responses (PDF p. 3, 2.2, 2nd paragraph). Item wording and case-ascertainment details are in Supplements S1-S3 (not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed in the paper; diagnosis is by algorithm from self-report items, without clinical assessment.
outcomes.operationalization: Attack rate: analysis-weighted number of initiates who became DSM-IV cocaine dependence cases between onset and assessment, divided by the analysis-weighted number of new initiates (PDF p. 3, 2.3, 1st paragraph); likewise for each problem item.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Dependence plus 21 problem items per subgroup; subgroup differences for items are reported as p below or above 0.05 without the test being described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Meta-analysis summaries of DSM-IV cocaine dependence within 12 months of onset: powder-only 5.0% (95% CI 4.0 to 6.3); powder-then-crack 22.2% (16.7 to 29.4) (PDF p. 2, Fig. 1; PDF p. 3, Results, 1st paragraph). Year-pair estimates: powder-only from 2.9% (1.8 to 4.7) in 2015-16 to 7.0% (5.3 to 9.2) in 2006-07; powder-then-crack from 10.3% (3.6 to 25.8) in 2008-09 to 30.0% (16.8 to 47.7) in 2006-07 and 30.0% (9.2 to 64.5) in 2015-16 (Fig. 1). Problem items: wanting or trying to cut down or stop, the most frequent, 45.4% (43.1 to 47.9) vs 58.3% (53.0 to 64.2), difference p < 0.05; continuing despite physical problems caused or worsened by cocaine, the least frequent, 1.9% (1.6 to 2.4) vs 2.8% (1.6 to 5.2), p > 0.05 (PDF p. 3, Results, 2nd paragraph). The authors call the ratio of the two summaries (22 to 5) a fourfold variation; it is 4.4. No adjusted estimates, no absolute differences with intervals. Editors' reconstruction from the rounded year-pair values in Fig. 1: DerSimonian-Laird random effects on the log scale reproduces both summaries exactly; heterogeneity chi-square about 14.4 (6 df, p about 0.03; I-squared about 58%) for powder-only and about 8.3 (6 df, p about 0.22; I-squared about 27%) for powder-then-crack; 95% prediction intervals about 2.6% to 9.9% and 12% to 41%; slope across year-pairs about zero for powder-then-crack (p about 0.96) and a decline for powder-only that is not significant once heterogeneity is allowed for (p about 0.08). Editors' reading of Fig. 2 bar heights by pixel measurement (agreeing within 0.2 points with the two values printed in the text): powder-only proportions below 10% for 17 of the 20 plotted items (the exceptions about 45%, 31% and 36%); powder-then-crack proportions 15% or more for 14 of the 20.
analysis.covariates: None, deliberately: frequency of use was left out as a likely mediator and collider (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 8th paragraph); no other covariates were considered.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only 2 of the 21 item estimates are given as numbers; the rest appear only as bars labelled SEPE1 to SEPE21, whose wording is in the supplement, and SEPE15 has no bar. Heterogeneity statistics, year-pair sample sizes and item forest plots are only in Supplements S2, S4 and S5 (not read).
analysis.power: Not discussed. Effective sample sizes of 9 to 96 per year-pair for powder-then-crack initiates give year-pair intervals as wide as 9.2% to 64.5%.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among people in US households who had started cocaine within the previous 12 months (2002-2016 surveys), an estimated 5% of those who had used only powder and 22% of those who had already gone on to crack met DSM-IV cocaine dependence criteria by the interview, and most of the 20 plotted dependence-related problems were reported more often by the powder-then-crack group, with exceptions. The comparison is unadjusted and the problems are not attributed to either form of cocaine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives three interpretations of the crack-associated excess (susceptibility predating onset, dependence leading to crack, greater toxicity of smoked crack) and calls the estimates preliminary in the Discussion, which matches the design (PDF p. 1; PDF p. 4). Gaps: (1) the abstract invites clinicians to use the estimates in a diagnostic workup when patients report starting cocaine (PDF p. 1), but the estimates are not standardized for time since onset; (2) the abstract calls the 22% risk statistically undifferentiable from the 30% reported for heroin by Rivera et al. (2018), without any test in the paper, and the crack interval (16.7% to 29.4%) does not include 30%; (3) the Results say the other items showed a crack-associated excess with one other exception, while Fig. 2 shows two items without excess, one of them higher in the powder-only group, and one item without an estimate (see reporting issues); (4) the Discussion sees some increase across years in the powder-then-crack estimates (PDF p. 3), which the year-pair values do not show (editors' trend check, slope about zero); (5) the Conclusions give the powder-then-crack risk as 20% (PDF p. 4) where the Results give 22%.

timeline.event: Wagner and Anthony: exposure opportunity and other mechanisms linking alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and cocaine use; cited for the suggestion that dealers selling powder may introduce people to crack (PDF p. 4).

Chen and Anthony, same research group, NHSDA 1995-1998: powder versus crack in the process of becoming dependent (title); cited here only as part of the evidence base (PDF p. 3). The project's first-pass card on it reports more dependence features among people who had recently started crack than among those who had started powder only.
Lopez-Quintero et al.: probability of transition from first use to dependence (NESARC); cited as part of the evidence base (PDF p. 3).
Rivera et al. (JAMA Psychiatry): same approach applied to newly incident heroin use, about 30% dependent within 12 months; the comparison in this paper's abstract; not appraised.
This short communication; the authors announce an analysis of the within-person dependence of the 21 items (Chandra and Anthony, in preparation) (PDF p. 3).

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the finding, more dependence features soon after onset among people who move on to crack, agrees with the same group's earlier analysis of 1995-1998 survey data as summarized on the project's first-pass card for chen_2004 (single features, adjusted models); the 5% and 22% figures themselves have no independent replication in the paper, and the three explanations the authors list remain untested.

Anthony (support in 2018); neither NIDA nor the university had any role in design, conduct, data handling, analysis, interpretation, preparation, review or approval of the manuscript, or the decision to submit (PDF p. 5, Role of the funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict declared (PDF p. 5, Declaration of Competing Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, College of Human Medicine, Michigan State University. Data from SAMHSA's restricted-access analysis system (PDF p. 5, Acknowledgements).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who have just started cocaine, recording the date of first use of each form, repeated assessments of dependence criteria and measures from before first use (other drug use, psychiatric and family history, social circumstances), analysed by time since onset; a case-crossover analysis of the months around first crack use, which the authors propose, would be a partial step.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National frame of non-institutionalized civilians aged 12 and over in households and group quarters; institutionalized people are not covered.
Multistage area probability sampling with analysis weights; design-based variance.
Adequate for powder-only initiates (3488 in total); small for powder-then-crack initiates (275 in total, 9 to 96 per year-pair), so year-pair estimates are imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: No characteristics of the initiates (age, sex, other drug use, time since onset) are reported.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Analysis weights are used, but how non-response and incomplete assessments were handled is not described; the authors acknowledge both problems.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: DSM-IV dependence derived from standardized self-report items; validity is not discussed and the item wording is only in the supplement; the items do not distinguish powder from crack.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same computer interview for all respondents within a survey year; comparability across 2002-2016 is not discussed and the 2014 survey is absent without explanation.

Design-based intervals and a meta-analysis of year-pair estimates are appropriate; but the test used to compare subgroups is not described, the stated fixed- or random-effects rule does not fit the powder-then-crack heterogeneity (editors' reconstruction), and nothing accounts for differing time since onset.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Participation above 65% each year, stated only globally; non-response adjustment is not described in the paper.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Editors' summary for the descriptive estimates: moderate risk of bias. They come from a large national probability survey with design-based intervals, but rest on self-reported diagnosis, unreported participant characteristics, an unstated and possibly unequal time since onset, and supplementary material that was not available. The JBI checklist is used because the card will support descriptive figures (the proportions meeting dependence criteria within a year of starting). For any causal reading of the difference between powder and crack, the comparison is unadjusted and confounded by pre-existing susceptibility, by time at risk and by the reverse sequence (dependence leading to crack), as the authors themselves say; judged with ROBINS-E that reading would be at very high risk of bias. Cite for: about 5% of US powder-only initiates and about 22% of powder-then-crack initiates meeting DSM-IV dependence criteria within 12 months of first use in NSDUH 2002-2016, and most dependence features being more common in the second group. Do not cite for: a toxic effect of smoking crack, a per-month risk, or equivalence with heroin.

key_findings.finding: Seven NSDUH year-pairs (2002-03 to 2012-13 and 2015-16) were analysed; unweighted effective sample sizes per year-pair were 194-590 powder-only and 9-96 powder-then-crack initiates, totalling 3488 and 275 in the abstract; each annual survey had more than 50,000 respondents with participation above 65%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Method (PDF p. 1); Fig. 1 (PDF p. 2); 2.1 Population and study design, 1st paragraph, and 2.3 Analyses, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Within 12 months of first cocaine use, 5.0% (95% CI 4.0 to 6.3) of powder-only initiates and 22.2% (16.7 to 29.4) of powder-then-crack initiates had become DSM-IV cocaine dependence cases (meta-analysis summaries of seven year-pairs).
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1, Panels A and B (PDF p. 2); Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3)
Fig. 1, Panels A and B, year-pair rows

key_findings.finding: Weighted projections of new initiates per year fell for powder-then-crack from 113,000 (2002-03) to 16,000 (2015-16), while powder-only initiates ranged from 597,000 to 1,017,000.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1, column of newly incident initiates (thousands)

key_findings.finding: The most frequent problem in both groups was wanting or trying to cut down or stop using cocaine: 45.4% (43.1 to 47.9) of powder-only vs 58.3% (53.0 to 64.2) of powder-then-crack initiates (p < 0.05). The least frequent, continuing despite physical problems caused or worsened by cocaine, was 1.9% (1.6 to 2.4) vs 2.8% (1.6 to 5.2), p > 0.05. The text states that the other items showed a crack-associated excess with one other exception, difficulty stopping cocaine use one or more times.

Fig. 2 plots bars for 20 of the 21 items; SEPE15 has no bar. Editors' reading of the bars: powder-only proportions are below 10% for 17 of the 20 items and powder-then-crack proportions are 15% or more for 14; SEPE6 is about equal in the two groups (about 3.7% vs 4.0%) and SEPE9 is higher in the powder-only group (about 36% vs 28%).
key_findings.note: Editors' reading by pixel measurement of the 300-dpi page; the method reproduces the two values printed in the text to within 0.2 points. The item wording behind each SEPE label is in Supplements S1-S3, which were not available, so the bars cannot be matched to named problems except the two given in the text (SEPE1 and SEPE14).

key_findings.finding: The authors give three explanations of the crack-associated excess without choosing between them: powder-then-crack initiates may start with greater susceptibility; some people may become dependent on powder and then start crack; or something about crack smoking (for example greater toxicity than insufflation) may raise the risk.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Conclusions (PDF p. 1); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (starts PDF p. 3, continues PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Frequency of use was deliberately not adjusted for, because the authors regard it as a mediator between crack use and dependence and as being increased by dependence.

The authors compare the 22% with an estimate that almost 1 in 3 (30%) people who had newly started heroin developed heroin dependence within 1-12 months, from Rivera et al. (2018) using essentially the same approach.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Conclusions (PDF p. 1); Conclusions, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say that, apart from the least frequent item, the items showed a crack-associated excess with one other exception; Fig. 2 shows two items without an excess, SEPE6 (about equal) and SEPE9 (about 36% powder-only vs 28% powder-then-crack, with 1-SE bars of about 1.3 and 1.8 points; editors' z about 3.6, a reversed difference), and SEPE15 without any estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one item is understated or unmentioned, and one item shows significantly more problems in the powder-only group; whether SEPE6 or SEPE9 is the item the text names cannot be settled without the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods state that fixed effects were used unless the heterogeneity chi-square was significant at 0.05, and Fig. 1 is titled random effects for both panels; the editors' reconstruction from Fig. 1 reproduces both summaries with random effects but finds heterogeneity chi-square of about 8.3 on 6 df (p about 0.22) for powder-then-crack, which by the stated rule calls for fixed effects (about 22.8%, 18.2 to 28.5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small numerical consequence; the heterogeneity tests themselves are only in Supplement S5, which was not available.

reporting_issues.issue: The year-pairs run 2002-03 to 2012-13 and then 2015-16, so 2014 is missing without explanation; the Fig. 2 caption gives the data years as 2002-2017 while Fig. 1, the abstract and the Methods give 2002-2016.
reporting_issues.consequence: The data years cannot be stated with certainty from the paper; comparability across survey years is not discussed.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract presents 3488 and 275 as the unweighted numbers of initiates, while the Methods describe the per-year-pair figures as effective sample sizes back-calculated from the RDAS output.
reporting_issues.consequence: The actual numbers of respondents are not given; the totals should be cited as the paper's effective sample sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the powder-then-crack risk (22%) statistically undifferentiable from the 30% heroin estimate, but no test is reported, and the 95% CI for crack (16.7% to 29.4%) does not include 30%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The equivalence statement is unsupported in this paper; the heroin estimate's own interval is not given.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says powder-then-crack estimates showed some increase across years; the year-pair values (16.9, 29.6, 30.0, 10.3, 14.4, 21.3, 30.0%) show no trend (editors' meta-regression slope about zero, p about 0.96). The Conclusions give the powder-then-crack risk as 20%, the Results 22%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The trend statement should not be cited; the risk should be cited as 22% (16.7% to 29.4%).

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction gives 50-135 people a day newly experiencing cocaine dependence in the US; the Conclusions split this into about 50 crack and 135 powder-only dependence cases a day and describe them as treatment caseload estimates; both are adapted from an initiation report (Lipari et al., 2017) without the calculation shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: These daily figures are second-hand and their derivation cannot be checked from the paper.

verification.source_read: Article-in-press PDF, 5 pages (journal volume and pages printed as xxx; anchors give the PDF's own page numbers, which may differ from the version of record, Drug Alcohol Depend 206:107717); all pages read; Figs 1 and 2, which are images, checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, Fig. 2 also at 300 dpi with bar heights measured; Fig. 1 summaries re-computed from the year-pair values; online Supplements S1-S5 not available and not read
